title: Nodes and pointers
objectives: Traverse and reverse a linked list.
Insert or delete after a node you hold in $O(1)$, and explain why indexing is $O(k)$
Use a dummy node so that removing the head needs no special case

screens.title: Only the next one
screens.prose: A **linked list** stores each value in a node. A node knows its value and the next node, nothing else. You hold one name, `head`, pointing at the first node.

params.aria: A linked list: circles are nodes, arrows are next pointers, pills are variable names

state.caption: Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node

screens.question: Tap every node you must visit, starting from `head`, to read the value 9.

hints.text: Can you jump straight to the third node?
You start here, at the node `head` points to.
From 7, `next` leads to 3, and from 3 it leads to 9. So you visit 7, 3 and 9.

feedback.correct: 7, then 3, then 9: one `next` at a time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at the node `head` points to and follow the arrows.

byKey.n1: You skipped 7. Every walk starts at `head`, which points to 7.
byKey.n2: You skipped 3. The only way from 7 to 9 is through 3.
byKey.n3: 9 is the value you want, so you visit its node too.
byKey.n4: 4 comes after 9. You can stop once you reach 9.

explain.text: You could not jump to 9: a node knows only its successor. Reading the $k$-th value means visiting $k$ nodes, so there is no $O(1)$ indexing. In code: `cur = head`, then `cur = cur.next` until you get there.

screens.title: Insert after a node
screens.prose: You hold `a`, the node with 3. You want 5 between 3 and 9. Two pointers must change: `new.next` and `a.next`.

params.aria: A linked list: circles are nodes, arrows are next pointers, pills are variable names

state.caption: `new = Node(5)` is not linked in yet

screens.question: Which order of the two lines works?

options.why: Once `a.next` is `new`, the second line sets `new.next = new`. The link to 9 is gone.

canvas.caption: 5 points at itself; 9 and 4 are lost

options.why: The order matters. Setting `a.next` first overwrites the only pointer to 9 before it is copied.

hints.text: After `a.next = new`, what does `a.next` point to?
This arrow is the only way to reach 9 from 3.
Copy the link to 9 into `new.next` first. Only then point `a.next` at `new`.

feedback.correct: Save the link to the rest of the list before you overwrite it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which line would destroy the only path to 9?

byKey.b: You overwrote `a.next` first. The second line then copies `new` into `new.next`, a loop, and 9 is unreachable.
byKey.c: The order matters: the other way round loses the rest of the list.

explain.text: `new.next = a.next` makes 5 point at 9. Then `a.next = new` makes 3 point at 5. Two pointer changes, whatever the list's length: $O(1)$.

screens.title: Against a Python list
screens.prose: A Python list stores its values side by side. `prices.insert(1, x)` puts `x` at index 1, so everything after it must move up one place.

params.aria: A linked list: circles are nodes, arrows are next pointers, pills are variable names

screens.question: How many values does `prices.insert(1, x)` move in a list of 1,000,000 prices?

hints.text: Which values sit at index 1 or later?
Only the value at index 0 stays where it is.
Indices 1 to 999,999 each shift up by one: that is 999,999 values.

feedback.correct: 999,999 values shift; the linked list changed two pointers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the values at index 1 or beyond.

byKey.all: The value at index 0 stays put. Every other value moves.
byKey.two: Two is the linked list's count of pointer changes. A Python list moves the values themselves.
byKey.one: Every value after index 1 shifts as well, not just one.

explain.text: The Python list moves 999,999 values: $O(n)$. The linked list changed two pointers: $O(1)$. The catch is that you must already hold `a`; finding it by walking from `head` is $O(n)$.

screens.title: Delete after a node
screens.prose: Now remove 9. You hold `a`, the node before it. A node cannot be erased in place; it disappears when nothing points to it any more.

params.aria: A linked list: circles are nodes, arrows are next pointers, pills are variable names

screens.question: Which single line removes 9 and keeps 4?

options.why: That cuts the list after 3, so 4 is lost along with 9.
That moves the name `a` to 4. No arrow between nodes changes, so 9 is still in the list.
That deletes the attribute from `a`'s node, so 3 has no `next` at all. The next walk raises `AttributeError`.

hints.text: Which arrow has to change so that 3 leads straight to 4?
Change where this arrow points.
`a.next.next` is the node with 4. Point `a.next` at it, and nothing points to 9 any more.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Change the arrow out of 3 so it skips 9.

byKey.b: You cut the list after 3. Setting `a.next` to `None` drops 4 too.
byKey.c: You moved the name `a`. Rebinding a name never changes an arrow between nodes.

explain.text: `a.next.next` is the node with 4, so 3 now skips 9. No name or node points to 9, and Python frees it. Removing the head is the edge case: no node comes before it, so write `head = head.next`.

screens.title: Reverse in place
screens.prose: To reverse the list, walk it once and turn each arrow round. Three names do it: `prev` (the part already reversed), `cur` (the node being turned) and `nxt` (the rest).

params.aria: Reversing a linked list with prev, cur and nxt

screens.question: Put the four lines of the loop body in order.

lines.text: `nxt = cur.next`, keep hold of the rest
`prev = cur`, the reversed part grows by one
`cur = nxt`, move on to the rest

hints.text: Which line would lose the rest of the list if it ran first?
This arrow is the only way from 1 to 2, 3 and 4.
Save `nxt` first. Then flip `cur.next`. Then advance `prev` before `cur`, since `prev` takes `cur`'s old value.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Nothing may overwrite `cur.next` before it is saved, and `prev` must take `cur` before `cur` moves.

byKey.flip: `cur.next = prev` destroys the only link to the rest. Save it in `nxt` first.
byKey.cur: If `cur` moves before `prev = cur`, `prev` jumps to the wrong node.

explain.text: After one pass of the body, 1 points to `None`, `prev` is 1 and `cur` is 2. The loop runs while `cur` is not `None`, then returns `prev`, the new head. Each node is visited once: $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space.

canvas.caption: After one step: None ← 1, and `cur` is 2

screens.title: One line short
screens.prose:
This version drops the `nxt` name to save a line.

```python
def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = cur.next
    return prev
```

params.aria: A linked list: circles are nodes, arrows are next pointers, pills are variable names

screens.question: What list does it return for 7 → 3 → 9 → 4?

options.why: That is what the right version returns. Here `cur.next` is overwritten before `cur = cur.next` reads it.
After the first pass `cur.next` is `None`, so `cur` becomes `None` and the loop stops.
Nothing reads `.next` from `None`: the loop stops as soon as `cur` is `None`.

hints.text: After `cur.next = prev` on the first pass, what is `cur.next`?
This arrow is overwritten on the first pass.
On the first pass `cur.next` becomes `None`. Then `cur = cur.next` sets `cur` to `None`, and the loop ends with `prev` at 7.

feedback.correct: The rest of the list was lost on the first pass.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the first pass line by line.

byKey.b: You expected it to work. `cur.next` is overwritten with `None` before `cur = cur.next` reads it.
byKey.c: `cur` becomes `None` after one pass, so the loop ends at once.

explain.text: The first pass sets 7's `next` to `None`, then reads that `None` back as the next node. The loop ends after one node, and 3, 9 and 4 are unreachable. Save `nxt = cur.next` before you overwrite it.

canvas.caption: 7 → None; the other three nodes are lost

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
You walked, inserted, deleted and reversed by moving pointers:

```python
new.next = a.next; a.next = new   # insert, O(1)
a.next = a.next.next              # delete, O(1)
cur = cur.next                    # walk one step
```

The rule behind every line: read a pointer before you overwrite it.
screens.question: Which job is $O(1)$ for a linked list but $O(n)$ for a Python list?

options.text: Insert a value just after a node you already hold

options.why: That is $O(1)$ for a Python list and $O(k)$ for a linked list, which has to walk.

options.text: Append at the end, given only the head
options.why: A Python list appends in $O(1)$. A linked list with only `head` must walk to the end first.

options.text: Find the node holding a given value
options.why: Both have to look through the values one by one: $O(n)$ each.

feedback.correct: Holding the node is what makes the linked list cheap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which job needs no walking and no shifting on a linked list?

explain.text: Inserting after a held node changes two pointers, while a Python list shifts everything behind the gap. For indexing and appending, the Python list wins. Pick the structure for the operation you do most.

screens.title: Write reverse
screens.prose: A hidden `Node` class is ready: `Node(val, next=None)`, with fields `val` and `next`. `from_list([7, 3])` builds 7 → 3 and returns its head; `to_list(head)` turns a list of nodes back into a Python list.

params.aria: Reversing a linked list with prev, cur and nxt

screens.question: Write `reverse(head)`: reverse the list in place and return the new head.

widget.starter:
# Node(val, next=None), from_list(values) and to_list(head) are ready to use.

def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    ...
widget.solution:
def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    return prev
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests: an empty list (`None`), one node, two nodes, and 100,000 nodes. Tests 6 and 7 check that the same nodes were re-linked, not copied.

hints.text: What does the loop body need to save before it flips an arrow?
`cur` starts at the head; `prev` starts at `None`.
`while cur:` then `nxt = cur.next`, `cur.next = prev`, `prev = cur`, `cur = nxt`. After the loop, `return prev`.

feedback.correct: Each arrow turned round once, in one pass.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `[4, 9, 3, 7]`. If you got `[7]`, you overwrote `cur.next` before saving it.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 passes `None`, an empty list. The `while cur:` loop should simply not run, and `prev` is `None`.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 checks that the original nodes were re-linked. Building new nodes uses $O(n)$ extra space.

explain.text: An empty list skips the loop and returns `None`; one node returns itself. The same nodes are re-linked, so the extra space is three names: $O(1)$.

canvas.caption: `return prev`: the old tail is the new head

screens.title: The second from the end
screens.prose: To remove the $n$-th node from the end in one pass, put a dummy node before the head. Start `fast` and `slow` on the dummy. Move `fast` $n + 1$ steps, then move both until `fast` is `None`. Here $n = 2$.

params.aria: A list with a dummy node in front

state.caption: A dummy node D sits before the head

screens.question: Tap the node where `slow` stops.

hints.text: Where is `fast` after its $n + 1 = 3$ steps?
After 3 steps from D, `fast` is on 9.
Then both move together: `fast` goes to 4, then `None`, while `slow` goes to 7, then 3. `slow` stops on 3, just before 9.

feedback.correct: `slow` stops on 3, so `slow.next` is 9, the second from the end.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move `fast` 3 steps first, then move both one step at a time.

byKey.n3: You moved `fast` only $n = 2$ steps. Then `slow` lands on the node to remove, but you need the node before it.
byKey.n1: `slow` moves on while `fast` walks from 9 to `None`: two more steps from D.
byKey.dummy: `slow` moves too, once `fast` is 3 steps ahead.
byKey.n4: `slow` stays 3 steps behind `fast`, so it cannot reach the tail.

explain.text: `fast` keeps a gap of $n + 1$, so `slow` stops one node before the target. Then `slow.next = slow.next.next` removes 9. The dummy matters when the target is the head: `slow` stays on D, and we return `dummy.next`.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests: a single node, the head ($n$ equal to the length) and the tail ($n = 1$). $n$ is always between 1 and the length.

hints.text: How far ahead of `slow` must `fast` be when `fast` reaches `None`?
Both start on the dummy, before the head.
`fast = slow = dummy`; move `fast` $n + 1$ times; `while fast:` move both; then `slow.next = slow.next.next` and `return dummy.next`.

feedback.correct: One pass, and the head is no special case.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 removes the second from the end. If 5 vanished instead of 4, `fast` started only $n$ ahead: give it $n + 1$ steps.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 removes the head of `[1, 2]`. Return `dummy.next`, not `head`, which still points at the removed node.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 removes the only node. The answer is an empty list, so `dummy.next` must become `None`.

explain.text: With $n$ equal to the length, `fast` reaches `None` straight away and `slow` stays on the dummy. Then `slow.next = slow.next.next` drops the head, and `dummy.next` is the new head. Without a dummy that case needs its own `if`.

screens.title: Cancelling a resting order
screens.prose: This exchange keeps each price level as a queue of resting orders. It expects many cancels, so each node has both `prev` and `next`: a **doubly linked list**. A dictionary maps each order id to its node. Order B is cancelled.

params.aria: Resting orders at one price, doubly linked, with a dictionary from order id to node

state.caption: Each order has `prev` and `next`; a dict maps order id to node

screens.question: Which update removes B in $O(1)$?

options.text: Walk from the front of the level until you reach B, then unlink it
options.why: That works, but it is $O(n)$ in the queue's length. The dict already hands you B's node.
A now skips B, but C's `prev` still points at B. Walking backwards would find the cancelled order.

options.text: Rebuild the level as a Python list without B
options.why: That copies every order: $O(n)$ per cancel.

hints.text: Which two arrows point at B?
The dictionary gives you B's node without any walking.
Look up B in the dict. Point A's `next` at C, and C's `prev` at A. Then nothing reaches B.

feedback.correct: Two pointer changes and a dict lookup: $O(1)$, however long the queue.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You hold the node; change both arrows that lead into it.

byKey.b: You walked to B. The dict lookup makes the walk unnecessary, which is what keeps cancels $O(1)$.
byKey.c: You fixed the forward arrow only. C still points back at B through `prev`.

explain.text: The dict finds B in $O(1)$, and `prev` gives its neighbour without walking. Unlinking takes two pointer changes, so a cancel costs the same in a queue of 5 or 50,000. The same pairing, a dict plus a doubly linked list, builds an LRU cache in the homework.

canvas.caption: A ⇄ C; B is gone from the level

ideas: A linked list is nodes joined by `next` pointers. There is no indexing: reaching the $k$-th node takes $k - 1$ steps from the head.
Holding a node, you insert or delete next to it by changing two pointers: $O(1)$. A Python list shifts items instead: $O(n)$.
Read a pointer before you overwrite it: reversal saves `nxt` first, and insertion sets `new.next` before `a.next`.

quiz.prose: An LRU cache holds the 1,000 most recently used prices and evicts the least recently used one when full. Every lookup moves that item to the front.
quiz.question: Why pair a dict with a doubly linked list?

options.text: The dict finds the node in $O(1)$; the list moves it to the front and drops the back in $O(1)$
The list makes lookups by key fast
options.why: Finding a key in a linked list means walking it: $O(n)$. The dict does the finding.

options.text: A dict alone keeps no order of use
options.why: That is part of it, but a plain Python list could keep the order. The point is that its moves cost $O(n)$, and the linked list's cost $O(1)$.

options.text: The list saves memory over the dict
options.why: It adds memory: two pointers per item. It is there for speed.

feedback.correct: Each half does the job the other is slow at.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which part finds, and which part reorders?

explain.text: The dict maps key to node, so you hold the node at once. Unlinking it and relinking at the front changes a few pointers, and eviction removes the tail. Every operation is $O(1)$.
